claim: Nematostella vectensis possesses a large number of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Cnidarians possess a large number of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) – the most common receptors of bilaterian neuropeptides – but most of these remain orphan with no known ligands.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about cnidarians.

claim: Most cnidarian GPCRs remain orphan with no known ligands.
source: Cnidarians possess a large number of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) – the most common receptors of bilaterian neuropeptides – but most of these remain orphan with no known ligands.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: A library of 64 peptides derived from 33 precursors was created for Nematostella vectensis.
source: We searched for neuropeptides in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis and created a library of 64 peptides derived from 33 precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result of the study.

claim: 31 Nematostella vectensis receptors were identified that are specifically activated by 1 to 3 of 14 peptides.
source: In a large-scale pharmacological screen with these peptides and 161 N. vectensis GPCRs, we identified 31 receptors specifically activated by 1 to 3 of 14 peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result of the pharmacological screen.

claim: 161 N. vectensis GPCRs were tested in a large-scale pharmacological screen.
source: In a large-scale pharmacological screen with these peptides and 161 N. vectensis GPCRs, we identified 31 receptors specifically activated by 1 to 3 of 14 peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as part of the experimental design.

claim: Cnidarian tissues are extensively connected by multilayer peptidergic networks.
source: Mapping GPCR and neuropeptide expression to single-cell sequencing data revealed how cnidarian tissues are extensively connected by multilayer peptidergic networks.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from mapping expression data.

claim: There is no direct orthology between cnidarian and bilaterian peptidergic systems.
source: Phylogenetic analysis identified no direct orthology to bilaterian peptidergic systems and supports the independent expansion of neuropeptide signaling in cnidarians from a few ancestral peptide-receptor pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result of phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Neuropeptide signaling in cnidarians expanded independently from a few ancestral peptide-receptor pairs.
source: Phylogenetic analysis identified no direct orthology to bilaterian peptidergic systems and supports the independent expansion of neuropeptide signaling in cnidarians from a few ancestral peptide-receptor pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The origin of neuropeptides predates the emergence of neurons.
source: The origin of neuropeptides predates the emergence of neurons and it is believed that these signaling molecules have been utilized in the most ancestral nervous systems (Jékely, 2021; Moroz et al., 2021; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Neuropeptide-like molecules occur in all major animal clades with neurons.
source: Neuropeptide-like molecules occur in all major animal clades with neurons, the Bilateria, Cnidaria, and Ctenophora, and even in the neuron-less Placozoa and Porifera (Hayakawa et al., 2022; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2019; Nikitin, 2015; Sachkova et al., 2021; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Neuropeptide-like molecules occur in neuron-less Placozoa and Porifera.
source: Neuropeptide-like molecules occur in all major animal clades with neurons, the Bilateria, Cnidaria, and Ctenophora, and even in the neuron-less Placozoa and Porifera (Hayakawa et al., 2022; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2019; Nikitin, 2015; Sachkova et al., 2021; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Most mature bioactive neuropeptides are 3–20 amino acids long.
source: Most mature bioactive neuropeptides are 3–20 amino acids long and derive from longer proneuropeptide precursors through cleavage and other post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Neuropeptides derive from longer proneuropeptide precursors through cleavage and other post-translational modifications.
source: Most mature bioactive neuropeptides are 3–20 amino acids long and derive from longer proneuropeptide precursors through cleavage and other post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The same set of enzymes are involved in proneuropeptide processing across animals.
source: The same set of enzymes are involved in proneuropeptide processing across animals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Prohormone convertases recognize dibasic cleavage sites flanking the active peptides.
source: These include prohormone convertases, which recognize dibasic cleavage sites flanking the active peptides, and peptidyl-glycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase, which converts C-terminal glycine residues to amide groups (Chufán et al., 2009; Seidah, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Peptidyl-glycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase converts C-terminal glycine residues to amide groups.
source: These include prohormone convertases, which recognize dibasic cleavage sites flanking the active peptides, and peptidyl-glycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase, which converts C-terminal glycine residues to amide groups (Chufán et al., 2009; Seidah, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Proneuropeptide precursors can contain a single peptide or multiple copies of identical or divergent peptide sequences separated by cleavage sites.
source: Proneuropeptide precursors can contain a single peptide or multiple copies of identical or divergent peptide sequences separated by cleavage sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Propeptide sequences evolve relatively rapidly.
source: The often repetitive structure and the presence of short active sequences interspersed with less-constrained interpeptide regions allow propeptide sequences to evolve relatively rapidly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from structural features.

claim: With increasing evolutionary distances it becomes hard or impossible to recognize orthologous proneuropeptide sequences.
source: Consequently, with increasing evolutionary distances it often becomes hard or impossible to recognize orthologous proneuropeptide sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of rapid evolution.

claim: Most neuropeptides signal through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Most neuropeptides signal through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are larger seven-transmembrane proteins that show a slower evolutionary rate than proneuropeptide precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: GPCRs show a slower evolutionary rate than proneuropeptide precursors.
source: Most neuropeptides signal through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are larger seven-transmembrane proteins that show a slower evolutionary rate than proneuropeptide precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: There is a strong pattern of coevolution between receptor and ligand in neuropeptide systems.
source: The cases where the evolution of both the proneuropeptides and their receptors could be reconstructed revealed a strong pattern of coevolution between receptor and ligand (Elphick et al., 2018; Escudero Castelán et al., 2022; Grimmelikhuijzen and Hauser, 2012; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Yañez-Guerra and Elphick, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: More than 30 conserved peptidergic signaling systems exist across bilaterians.
source: These analyses revealed more than 30 conserved peptidergic signaling systems across bilaterians (Elphick et al., 2018; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Thiel et al., 2021; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The nervous system of cnidarians is strongly peptidergic.
source: The nervous system of cnidarians has long been known to be strongly peptidergic and proneuropeptides have been found across all major cnidarian clades (Koch et al., 2021; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Proneuropeptides have been found across all major cnidarian clades.
source: The nervous system of cnidarians has long been known to be strongly peptidergic and proneuropeptides have been found across all major cnidarian clades (Koch et al., 2021; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Most cnidarian neuropeptides are short amidated peptides.
source: Most cnidarian neuropeptides are short amidated peptides, resembling those found in bilaterians.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Three proneuropeptide families were present in the cnidarian stem lineage.
source: Genomic comparisons revealed three proneuropeptide families that were present in the cnidarian stem lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a result of genomic comparisons.

claim: GLWamides, GRFamides, and PRXamides are three proneuropeptide families present in the cnidarian stem lineage.
source: Genomic comparisons revealed three proneuropeptide families that were present in the cnidarian stem lineage. All three give rise to short amidated neuropeptides: GLWamides, GRFamides, and PRXamides (with 'X' representing a variable amino acid residue) (Koch et al., 2021; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: QITRFamide and HIRamide are specific to Hexacorallia.
source: Other neuropeptides are more specific to certain cnidarian groups such as QITRFamide and HIRamide to Hexacorallia or LRWamides to Anthozoa (Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: LRWamides are specific to Anthozoa.
source: Other neuropeptides are more specific to certain cnidarian groups such as QITRFamide and HIRamide to Hexacorallia or LRWamides to Anthozoa (Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Peptides orthologous between bilaterians and cnidarians are restricted to a few atypical neuropeptides.
source: Peptides that are sufficiently similar to be considered orthologous between bilaterians and cnidarians are restricted to a few atypical neuropeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of current knowledge.

claim: Insulin-related peptides, glycoprotein-hormone-related peptides, trunk-related peptides, nesfatin, and phoenixin are orthologous between bilaterians and cnidarians.
source: These include insulin-related peptides, glycoprotein-hormone-related peptides, trunk-related peptides, nesfatin, and phoenixin (de Oliveira et al., 2019; Roch and Sherwood, 2014; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Common short amidated peptides have no clear orthologs between cnidarians and bilaterians.
source: The more common short amidated peptides, however, have no clear orthologs in bilaterians.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of current knowledge.

claim: Receptors for Hydra vulgaris RFamide peptides have been identified.
source: Receptors for most cnidarian neuropeptides are still unknown, with two exceptions. These include receptors for Hydra vulgaris RFamide peptides and a receptor for a PRXamide maturation-inducing hormone (MIH) in the hydrozoan Clytia hemisphaerica (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020; Assmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A receptor for a PRXamide maturation-inducing hormone (MIH) in Clytia hemisphaerica has been identified.
source: Receptors for most cnidarian neuropeptides are still unknown, with two exceptions. These include receptors for Hydra vulgaris RFamide peptides and a receptor for a PRXamide maturation-inducing hormone (MIH) in the hydrozoan Clytia hemisphaerica (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020; Assmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hydra RFamide peptides activate heterotrimeric peptide-gated ion channels belonging to the DEG/ENaC family.
source: Hydra RFamide peptides activate heterotrimeric peptide-gated ion channels belonging to the DEG/ENaC family and distantly related to bilaterian RFamide- and Wamide-gated ion channels (Dandamudi et al., 2022; Elkhatib et al., 2022; Gründer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The Clytia MIH receptor is a class A GPCR.
source: The Clytia MIH receptor is a class A GPCR, which together with related cnidarian GPCRs shows a many-to-many ortholog relationship to a range of bilaterian neuropeptide GPCR families that also contain receptors for RFamide-like neuropeptides (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: The Clytia MIH receptor shows a many-to-many ortholog relationship to a range of bilaterian neuropeptide GPCR families.
source: The Clytia MIH receptor is a class A GPCR, which together with related cnidarian GPCRs shows a many-to-many ortholog relationship to a range of bilaterian neuropeptide GPCR families that also contain receptors for RFamide-like neuropeptides (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: The genome of Nematostella vectensis contains over 1000 GPCR genes.
source: The genome of the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, for example, contains over 1000 GPCR genes (Krishnan and Schiöth, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Earlier analyses suggested direct orthologous relationships between several cnidarian and bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs.
source: Earlier analyses suggested direct orthologous relationships between several cnidarian and bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs such as orexin/allatotropin, somatostatin or neuropeptide Y receptors, besides others (Alzugaray et al., 2013; Anctil, 2009; Krishnan and Schiöth, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: More recent phylogenies suggest that cnidarian neuropeptide GPCRs are more closely related to each other than to bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs.
source: More recent and comprehensive phylogenies suggest that cnidarian neuropeptide GPCRs are more closely related to each other than to bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs and only show many-to-many, or few-to-many orthology with bilaterian receptors (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020; Hauser et al., 2022; Thiel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of cnidarian GPCRs is still lacking.
source: However, a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of cnidarian GPCRs is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: N-terminal peptide cleavage occurs at dibasic KR-x, RR-x, and KK-x sites in Nematostella.
source: MS confirmed the occurrence of N-terminal peptide cleavage at dibasic KR-x, RR-x, and KK-x sites, with 'x' indicating the N-terminal amino acid of the resulting active peptide (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cleavage at dibasic sites is typical for bilaterian precursors.
source: Cleavage at such dibasic sites is typical for bilaterian precursors (Southey et al., 2008; Veenstra, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: In Nematostella, the cleavage site is often followed by a Q residue as the most N-terminal amino acid of the peptide.
source: In Nematostella, the cleavage site is often followed by a Q residue as the most N-terminal amino acid of the peptide (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Some Nematostella peptides are processed by cleavage N-terminal to a Q residue without any basic residue.
source: Our MS data showed that some peptides are processed by cleavage N-terminal to a Q residue without any basic residue but the cleavage site is instead often accompanied by an acidic (D or E) residue 1 or 2 positions N-terminal of the cleavage site (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: C-terminal peptide cleavage occurs at dibasic x-KR, x-RR, x-KK sites in Nematostella.
source: C-terminal peptide cleavage occurs at dibasic x-KR, x-RR, x-KK and in some cases at alternative monobasic Rxx-R sites, with a second basic amino acid 3 positions N-terminal of the cleavage site (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C-terminal cleavage in Nematostella is similar to that found in bilaterian propeptides.
source: This is similar to the C-terminal cleavage found in bilaterian propeptides (Southey et al., 2008; Veenstra, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Peptide alpha-amidation occurs by the conversion of a C-terminal glycine residue to an amide group in Nematostella.
source: In many neuropeptides, we could also confirm peptide alpha-amidation by the conversion of a C-terminal glycine residue to an amide group.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as confirmed by mass spectrometry.

claim: 15 new neuropeptide precursors were identified in N. vectensis.
source: Our screen complements the list of known neuropeptides in N. vectensis (Hayakawa et al., 2022; Hayakawa et al., 2019; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020) with 15 new neuropeptide precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the screen.

claim: The number of GPCRs across Metazoa varies by species and does not correlate with phylogenetic affiliation.
source: The number of GPCRs across Metazoa varies by species and seems not to correlate with phylogenetic affiliation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: 1061 class A GPCR sequences were initially detected from combined N. vectensis transcriptomes.
source: From the combined N. vectensis transcriptomes (see Supplementary file 5), we initially detected a total of 1061 class A GPCR sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the analysis.

claim: Only a few well-connected clusters of receptors are conserved across all major metazoan lineages.
source: This revealed only a few well-connected clusters of receptors conserved across all major metazoan lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Leucine-rich-repeat containing (lrrc) GPCRs are receptors for larger peptides such as bursicons and related glycoprotein hormones or for relaxins and related insulin-like peptides.
source: These include the leucine-rich-repeat containing (lrrc) GPCRs, which are receptors for larger peptides such as bursicons and related glycoprotein hormones or for relaxins and related insulin-like peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: In the two major GPCR clusters, cnidarian and bilaterian sequences form separate subclusters.
source: In both major clusters, cnidarian and bilaterian sequences form separate subclusters, rather than cnidarian GPCRs being interspersed with bilaterian GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the cluster analysis.

claim: One major GPCR cluster contains bilaterian GPCRs for low-molecular-weight neurotransmitters.
source: One of these clusters contains bilaterian GPCRs for low-molecular-weight neurotransmitters, including monoamines, trace amines, acetylcholine, melatonin, and ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the cluster analysis.

claim: The second major GPCR cluster contains most bilaterian neuropeptide receptors.
source: The second major cluster contains most bilaterian neuropeptide receptors (Figure 2C – neuropeptide II, III, gamma) as well as the bilaterian-specific chemokine, purinergic-P2Y, and fatty acid receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: 161 Nematostella GPCR sequences were selected for testing.
source: Based on this cluster analysis, we selected 161 Nematostella GPCR sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as part of the experimental design.

claim: GLWL peptide activates a single receptor (R18) with EC50=9E-7.
source: The neuropeptides GLWL, PFHamide, VRHamide, and QWamide each activate a different, single receptor (GLWL/R18 EC50=9E-7, PFHa/R36 EC50=1.2E-8, VRHa/R186 EC50=2.7E-10, QWa/R69 EC50=9E-7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: PFHamide peptide activates a single receptor (R36) with EC50=1.2E-8.
source: The neuropeptides GLWL, PFHamide, VRHamide, and QWamide each activate a different, single receptor (GLWL/R18 EC50=9E-7, PFHa/R36 EC50=1.2E-8, VRHa/R186 EC50=2.7E-10, QWa/R69 EC50=9E-7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: VRHamide peptide activates a single receptor (R186) with EC50=2.7E-10.
source: The neuropeptides GLWL, PFHamide, VRHamide, and QWamide each activate a different, single receptor (GLWL/R18 EC50=9E-7, PFHa/R36 EC50=1.2E-8, VRHa/R186 EC50=2.7E-10, QWa/R69 EC50=9E-7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: QWamide peptide activates a single receptor (R69) with EC50=9E-7.
source: The neuropeptides GLWL, PFHamide, VRHamide, and QWamide each activate a different, single receptor (GLWL/R18 EC50=9E-7, PFHa/R36 EC50=1.2E-8, VRHa/R186 EC50=2.7E-10, QWa/R69 EC50=9E-7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: HRPamide and FRPamide peptides activate the same single receptor R248.
source: Peptides ending in RPamide from the HRPamide and FRPamide precursors activate the same, single receptor R248.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: HRPamide activates R248 with EC50=8.9E-9.
source: The HRPa peptide has a lower EC50 value, the FRPa peptide, however, has a lower threshold activation while reaching its maximum activation at higher concentrations with an overall more shallow curve slope (HRPa/R248 EC50=8.9E-9, HRPa/R248 slope = 1.75, FRPa/R248 EC50=2.3E-7, FRPa/R248 slope = 0.42) (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: FRPamide activates R248 with EC50=2.3E-7.
source: The HRPa peptide has a lower EC50 value, the FRPa peptide, however, has a lower threshold activation while reaching its maximum activation at higher concentrations with an overall more shallow curve slope (HRPa/R248 EC50=8.9E-9, HRPa/R248 slope = 1.75, FRPa/R248 EC50=2.3E-7, FRPa/R248 slope = 0.42) (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: pyrQGRFamide activates receptors R70 and R234.
source: The RFamide peptides with the sequence pyrQGRFamide and pyrQITRFamide are each encoded on separate precursors and despite their strong sequence similarities each activate separate receptors (pyrQGRFa/R70 EC50=2.1E-6, pyrQGRFa/R234 EC50=4.7E-9, pyrQITRFa/R196 EC50=7.7E-11) although one of the two pyrQGRFamide receptors is also activated by higher concentrations of pyrQITRFamide (QITRFa/R70 EC50=1.7E-5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: pyrQITRFamide activates receptor R196 with EC50=7.7E-11.
source: The RFamide peptides with the sequence pyrQGRFamide and pyrQITRFamide are each encoded on separate precursors and despite their strong sequence similarities each activate separate receptors (pyrQGRFa/R70 EC50=2.1E-6, pyrQGRFa/R234 EC50=4.7E-9, pyrQITRFa/R196 EC50=7.7E-11) although one of the two pyrQGRFamide receptors is also activated by higher concentrations of pyrQITRFamide (QITRFa/R70 EC50=1.7E-5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: pyrQITRFamide also activates R70 at higher concentrations with EC50=1.7E-5.
source: The RFamide peptides with the sequence pyrQGRFamide and pyrQITRFamide are each encoded on separate precursors and despite their strong sequence similarities each activate separate receptors (pyrQGRFa/R70 EC50=2.1E-6, pyrQGRFa/R234 EC50=4.7E-9, pyrQITRFa/R196 EC50=7.7E-11) although one of the two pyrQGRFamide receptors is also activated by higher concentrations of pyrQITRFamide (QITRFa/R70 EC50=1.7E-5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: Two receptors (R21 and R29) are activated by HIRamide.
source: Two receptors are activated by HIRamide (R21 EC50=2.1E-9, R29 EC50=1.9E-7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: Four receptors (R26, R187, R197, R230) are activated by FLRNamide.
source: Four receptors are activated by FLRNamide (FLRNa/R26 EC50=7.4E-8, FLRNa/R187 EC50=7E-8, FLRNa/R197 EC50=1.1E-8, FLRNa/R230 EC50=4.7E-9), and one of these is also sensitive to higher concentrations of FYRVamide (FYRVa/R197 EC50=1.1E-6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: FYRVamide activates R197 at higher concentrations with EC50=1.1E-6.
source: Four receptors are activated by FLRNamide (FLRNa/R26 EC50=7.4E-8, FLRNa/R187 EC50=7E-8, FLRNa/R197 EC50=1.1E-8, FLRNa/R230 EC50=4.7E-9), and one of these is also sensitive to higher concentrations of FYRVamide (FYRVa/R197 EC50=1.1E-6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: Three LRWamide peptides (pyrQGLRWamide, pyrQGGLRWamide, GPPQGLRWamide) are each encoded as a single copy on separate precursors.
source: The three LRWamide peptides pyrQGLRWamide (LRWa1), pyrQGGLRWamide (LRWa2), and GPPQGLRWamide (LRWa3), which are each encoded as a single copy on separate precursors (Figure 1C), cross-activate four different GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: LRWamide peptides cross-activate four different GPCRs (R19, R193, R204, R213).
source: The three LRWamide peptides pyrQGLRWamide (LRWa1), pyrQGGLRWamide (LRWa2), and GPPQGLRWamide (LRWa3), which are each encoded as a single copy on separate precursors (Figure 1C), cross-activate four different GPCRs. Each LRWamide seems to have one preferred receptor (LRWa1/R19 EC50=9.1E-8, LRWa2/R213 EC50=3.1E-8, LRWa3/R204 EC50=7.4E-10) plus a fourth GPCR (R193) which appears similarly sensitive to all LRWamide peptides (LRWa1/R193 EC50=6.6E-11, LRWa2/R193 EC50=2E-10, LRWa3/R193 EC50=6.9E-10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: PRGamide activates at least 13 different receptors in Nematostella.
source: Finally, the PRGamide peptide, which belongs to the ancestral cnidarian PRXamides, activates at least 13 different receptors (R28, R32, R198, R199, R200, R202, R210, R211, R219, R220, R221, R222, R223) in Nematostella with EC50 values between 1.6E-10 and 4.5E-8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: PRGamide activates 13 receptors with EC50 values between 1.6E-10 and 4.5E-8.
source: Finally, the PRGamide peptide, which belongs to the ancestral cnidarian PRXamides, activates at least 13 different receptors (R28, R32, R198, R199, R200, R202, R210, R211, R219, R220, R221, R222, R223) in Nematostella with EC50 values between 1.6E-10 and 4.5E-8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of the pharmacological assay.

claim: At least nine neuropeptide GPCR families are ancestral to cnidarians.
source: Within the two cnidarian clusters, there are at least nine neuropeptide GPCR families that are ancestral to Cnidaria, all of which are represented with clear anthozoan and medusozoan orthology groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The deorphanized N. vectensis neuropeptide GPCRs belong to at least seven ancestral cnidarian families.
source: The deorphanized N. vectensis neuropeptide GPCRs belong to at least seven of these ancestral cnidarian families (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B and C.

claim: One cnidarian GPCR cluster expanded late within the Hexacorallia branch, with more than 100 GPCRs in N. vectensis.
source: One of the two main cnidarian clusters seems to have only expanded late within the Hexacorallia branch, with an especially high number of more than 100 GPCRs in N. vectensis (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B and C.

claim: The entire GPCR cluster is expanded in N. vectensis and Exaiptasia pallida, but not in Corallium rubrum or medusozoan species.
source: The entire cluster is expanded in N. vectensis and Exaiptasia pallida, but neither expanded in Corallium rubrum, nor in medusozoan species.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The second major cnidarian neuropeptide GPCR cluster contains at least eight ancestral cnidarian receptor families.
source: The second major cnidarian neuropeptide GPCR cluster contains at least eight ancestral cnidarian receptor families, based on the presence of clear anthozoan and medusozoan orthology groups, with deorphanized N. vectensis receptors in six of them (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B and C.

claim: The QITRFamide GPR196 belongs to a small group of hexacorallian receptors with no clear orthologs in C. rubrum or any medusozoan species.
source: The QITRFamide GPR196 belongs to a small group of hexacorallian receptors with no clear orthologs in C. rubrum or any medusozoan species, which might either represent a separate ancestral group with no medusozoan representative sequences or a strongly diverged Hexacorallia subcluster.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The QGRFamide GPR234 belongs to an ancestral cnidarian GPCR family.
source: The QGRFamide GPR234 belongs to an ancestral cnidarian GPCR family, which is in accordance with the existence of QGRFamide or GRFamide peptide precursors across Cnidaria (Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2020; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The receptors for LRWamide, FLRNamide, and HIRamide are closely related as part of an anthozoan/hexacorallian expansion.
source: The receptors for the peptides LRWamide, FLRNamide, and HIRamide are closely related as part of an anthozoan/hexacorallian expansion, curiously twice in unrelated families.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The 13 PRGamide receptors of N. vectensis belong to two separate ancestral cnidarian families.
source: The 13 PRGamide receptors of N. vectensis belong to two separate ancestral cnidarian families, both of which are expanded in anthozoans.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: One PRGamide family contains the Clytia MIH receptor which is activated by Clytia PRXamides.
source: The other PRGamide family contains the Clytia MIH receptor which is activated by Clytia PRXamides (Quiroga Artigas et al., 2020), confirming a peptide-receptor coevolution in cnidarians for the ancestral PRXamides (Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2019) and their receptor(s).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Most of the bilaterian and cnidarian class A neuropeptide GPCRs diversified after the bilaterian-cnidarian split.
source: Most of the bilaterian and cnidarian class A neuropeptide GPCRs therefore diversified after the bilaterian-cnidarian split.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The only family with an apparently consistent one-to-one orthology of an ancestral cnidarian and bilaterian branch of receptors is that of the bilaterian orphan receptor GPR19.
source: The only family with an apparently consistent one-to-one orthology of an ancestral cnidarian and bilaterian branch of receptors is that of the bilaterian orphan receptor GPR19.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Most neuropeptide precursors show restricted expression in neuroglandular cells.
source: Most neuropeptide precursors show restricted expression in neuroglandular cells (Figure 5B), with the exception of the phoenixin and GLWL precursors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The broad expression of phoenixin suggests other functions for this molecule outside neuronal signaling.
source: The broad expression of phoenixin suggests other functions for this molecule outside neuronal signaling, e.g., in mitochondrial regulation (Dennerlein et al., 2015; ; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from expression data with supporting citations.

claim: Individual GPCRs were often restricted to a single or very few tissue types.
source: Individual GPCRs were often restricted to a single or very few tissue types (Figure 5B for tissue-type overview and Supplementary file 12 for cell-type-specific resolution).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: For peptides with multiple receptors, distinct patterns of receptor expression were found.
source: For peptides with multiple receptors, we often found distinct patterns of receptor expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from expression data.

claim: Within the neuroglandular subset, each neuronal cell type expresses a unique combination of neuropeptide precursors and GPCRs.
source: Within the neuroglandular subset, each neuronal cell type expresses a unique combination of neuropeptide precursors and GPCRs (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3; Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Most peptide precursors are restricted to only a few cell types.
source: Most peptide precursors are thereby restricted to only a few cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from expression data.

claim: PRGamide is restricted to two types of neuroglandular cells: the larval apical organ N1.L2 cells and the N2.g1 cells.
source: PRGamide, for example, is restricted to two types of neuroglandular cells: the larval apical organ N1.L2 cells and the N2.g1 cells, which persist in adults (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The restricted expression of the PRGamide precursor is in accordance with previously published in situ hybridizations.
source: This restricted expression of the PRGamide precursor is also in accordance with previously published in situ hybridizations that show a restricted expression in the larval apical organ (Gilbert et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citation.

claim: The larval N1.L2 cells express the PRGamide, VRHamide, QITRFamide, RPamide, LRE peptide, GLWL peptide, and the phoenixin precursor.
source: The larval N1.L2 cells express the PRGamide, VRHamide, QITRFamide, RPamide, LRE peptide, GLWL peptide, and the phoenixin precursor, while only expressing two receptors: the PRGamide receptor R.200 with a lower average expression and the VRHamide receptor R186.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from expression data.

claim: The expression of both the PRGamide and VRHamide peptide precursors and receptors may indicate autocrine regulation in N1.L2 cells.
source: The expression of both the PRGamide and VRHamide peptide precursors and receptors may indicate autocrine regulation in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from expression data.

claim: The peptidergic network was subdivided into three (developmental) or four (adult) modules by modularity analysis.
source: By modularity analysis, we subdivided the networks into three (developmental) or four (adult) modules, each dominated by peptides with multiple receptors: PRGamide, pyrQGRFamide, FLRNamide, and LRWamide (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, E.

claim: The cells at the center of the peptidergic network modules are the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.L2, N1.L3, and N2.g1 cells in the developmental dataset.
source: The cells at the center of these modules that are most strongly involved in peptidergic signaling are the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.L2, N1.L3, and N2.g1 cells in the developmental dataset and the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.g2, and N2.g1 cells in the adult dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of network analysis.

claim: The cells at the center of the peptidergic network modules are the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.g2, and N2.g1 cells in the adult dataset.
source: The cells at the center of these modules that are most strongly involved in peptidergic signaling are the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.L2, N1.L3, and N2.g1 cells in the developmental dataset and the N1.g3, N1S.3, N1.g2, and N2.g1 cells in the adult dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a result of network analysis.

claim: The identified neuropeptide GPCRs belong to two major GPCR clades that expanded independently of each other.
source: Our phylogeny suggests that the identified neuropeptide GPCRs belong to two major GPCR clades that expanded independently of each other.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: One GPCR clade diversified in stem Cnidaria into eight receptor families that are all present across medusozoans and anthozoans.
source: One clade diversified in stem Cnidaria into eight receptor families that are all present across medusozoans and anthozoans.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The other GPCR clade diversified later within the anthozoans, likely from a single ancestral cnidarian receptor.
source: The other clade diversified later within the anthozoans, likely from a single ancestral cnidarian receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The expansion of GPCR systems is a general feature of GPCR evolution and happened independently in different lineages and at different times during animal evolution.
source: The expansion of GPCR systems is a general feature of GPCR evolution and happened independently in different lineages and at different times during animal evolution (Beets et al., 2022; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The cnidarian neuropeptide receptors show many-to-many orthology relationship to bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs.
source: The cnidarian neuropeptide receptors we identified here show many-to-many orthology relationship to bilaterian neuropeptide GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: No direct receptor orthologs were identified between cnidarians and bilaterians.
source: We did not identify any direct receptor orthologs between cnidarians and bilaterians, indicating extensive parallel expansion of neuropeptide signaling in the two clades.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Two N. vectensis RFamide receptors were identified, one for pyrQGRFamide and one for pyrQITRFamide.
source: We identified two N. vectensis RFamide receptors, one for the ancestral cnidarian neuropeptide pyrQGRFamide (Koch et al., 2021; Koch and Grimmelikhuijzen, 2019) and one for the hexacorallia pyrQITRFamide.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a result of the study.

claim: The two N. vectensis RFamide receptors belong to either of the two major clades of cnidarian receptors.
source: These two N. vectensis receptors belong to either of the two major clades of cnidarian receptors, suggesting that new RFamide receptors and/or peptides can evolve independently.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Within bilaterians there are many RFamides across protostomes and deuterostomes that are not orthologous to each other.
source: Likewise, within bilaterians there are many RFamides across protostomes and deuterostomes that are not orthologous to each other (Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014; Thiel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The cnidarian RFamide receptors are more closely related to other cnidarian neuropeptide receptors than to bilaterian RFamide receptors.
source: The cnidarian RFamide receptors are also more closely related to other cnidarian neuropeptide receptors than to bilaterian RFamide receptors, arguing against the orthology of cnidarian and bilaterian RFamides.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The orthology of six N. vectensis PRGamide receptors to the PRXamide receptor of Clytia hemisphaerica is the first example of long-term ligand-receptor association across cnidarians.
source: The orthology of six of the identified anthozoan N. vectensis PRGamide receptors to the PRXamide receptor of the hydrozoan C. hemisphaerica is the first example of a similar long-term ligand-receptor association across cnidarians.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Receptors of ancient peptides such as PRXamides or GRFamide are expected to be orthologous even in distantly related cnidarians.
source: Receptors of ancient peptides such as PRXamides or GRFamide are therefore expected to be orthologous even in distantly related cnidarians.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the findings.

claim: The unique combinations of proneuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors in different neuronal cell types can be used as markers to identify and characterize neuronal cell types.
source: The unique combinations of proneuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors in the different neuronal cell types can also be used as markers to identify and characterize neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an implication of the findings.

claim: The uniquely specific combinatorial expression of proneuropeptides as neuronal markers parallels the situation found in bilaterian nervous systems.
source: The uniquely specific combinatorial expression of proneuropeptides as neuronal markers parallels the situation found in bilaterian nervous systems, where proneuropeptides provide fingerprint-like identities to different neuronal cell types (Smith et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Receptors for peptides from nearly half of the Nematostella neuropeptide precursors were identified.
source: Overall, we identified receptors for peptides from nearly half of the Nematostella neuropeptide precursors, including the receptors of the ancient PRXamide and pyrQGRFamide peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the results.
